newsitem.title: ITALY: EU Commissioner warns against market euphoria.
newsitem.headline: EU Commissioner warns against market euphoria.

text.p: EU Commissioner Mario Monti warned Italy on Monday of the dangers of being swept away by euphoria as stock and bond prices soared to all-time highs on rising expectations that Italy will join a currency union.

"Since the end of 1996 Italy has made big progress but beware of being blinded by euphoria," Monti told Rome daily La Repubblica in an interview. He also said it was not a foregone conclusion that Italy would be let into the EMU club.

The government is engaged in a do-or-die bid to slash a large public sector deficit -- the biggest single obstacle to Italy being admitted to European economic and monetary union (EMU) -- and financial markets have been applauding all the way.
The Italian BTP September futures contract on the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) soared to a record high of 137.10 early on Monday before slipping back.
The all-share Mibtel index also climbed to its highest ever level at 14,154 as orders flooded in from foreign and domestic investors.

The buying frenzy on financial markets has been driven by so-called "convergence" trading as investors place huge bets on Italy being admitted to the first round of European economic and monetary union (EMU), planned for launch in 1999.

Market watchers now say that with the odds shortening on Italy's chances of qualifying for EMU straight away the one thing that could trigger a panic among investors would be a decision to delay the start of a currency union.

Monti, an influential figure who never hesitates to speak out if he feels Italy's resolve to streamline its economy shows signs of flagging, said joining a currency union union was not an automatic cure for Italy's economic ills.

Italy's success in cutting its public sector deficit, now widely expected to fall to three percent of gross domestic product this year, has diverted attention from the economy's Achilles heel -- an enormous national debt.

Just as Italy looks increasingly likely to meet the magic three percent target laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, which spells out conditions for EMU membership, France and Germany have been struggling to make the grade.

Monti said that Italy's national debt -- equivalent in size to 122 percent of GDP -- could come under closer scrutiny if the three percent rule is not applied too strictly when EU leaders decide next year which countries to admit to EMU.

"If in the eyes of German citizens a Euro (single currency) with everybody in it is a weak currency, then it is possible that political attention will shift to the criterion which until now has been overshadowed, that is, the national debt," he said.

The Maastricht Treaty states that EMU aspirants should have a national debt of no more than 60 percent of gross domestic product. Italy, although well above the debt threshold, still has a chance provided its debt is on a steady downward path.
Some people feared Italy, once inside EMU, could try to put pressure on the Eureopean central bank not to raise interest rates even if it were prudent to do so, said Monti.

Even after it is converted into the new single currency, the Euro, Italian debt would be very sensitive to interest rate swings because much of it is funded by treasury paper with short maturities, he added. "Italian public debt represents a very high proportion of total European debt," he said.
Italy could only dispel these worries if it proved its determination to cut the public debt permanently by pruning spending on state pensions and welfare, he added.
